subtopic: MR. BOUTIN  FAILURE TO FLY QUEBEC FLAG

speechtext: AT ROYAL 22ND REGIMENT CEREMONY [Translation]

subtopic: MR. BOUTIN  FAILURE TO FLY QUEBEC FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is based on an article published in the September 24 issue of the newspaper Le Droit and entitled: VanDoos allegedly refused permission to fly fleur-de-lis.
Presumably, the incident occurred during the ceremonies which took place on parliament hill Wednesday morning, to commemorate the 50th anniversary of this army unit. According to the press report, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) would have refused to let fleur-de-lis flags-the fleur-de-lis is the flag of the province of Quebec-be raised between the red ensigns placed around the national war memorial.
If such is the case, Mr. Speaker, I want to protest strongly against that insult and that outrage committed against the members of the Royal 22nd, a regiment almost entirely made up of French Canadians from the province of Quebec, in refusing them permission to fly the flag of their province during those ceremonies.
The Royal 22nd regiment is not the sole victim of that insult. The whole population of Quebec was insulted on that day.
Men of the VanDoos always conducted themselves as heroes in the various conflicts in which they took part. The valour, bravery and heroism of those French Canadians were reflected not only on the province of Quebec, but on Canada as a whole.
Again, today, it is the Royal 22nd which is entrusted with the peace keeping operations in Cyprus.
Everywhere and at all times the Royal 22nd has been a credit to Canada. It has produced thousands of heroes. It deserves better from the Canadian government than the insult to which it was subjected by the Department of National Defence last Wednesday.
Mr. Speaker, that was also an insult to French Canadians from Quebec and the other provinces. If my compatriots keep on being flouted as they were last Wednesday, the Quebec separatist movements will be justified up to a certain point.
Consequently, I would like the Minister of National Defence or, in his absence, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to explain or justify the refusal to fly the fleur-de-lis beside the red ensign during the ceremony commemorating the 50th anniversary of the foundation of the Royal 22nd, and to present apologies to that unit.

subtopic: MR. BOUTIN  FAILURE TO FLY QUEBEC FLAG
speechtext:
Order, please. I have to decide whether there is a question of privilege. This is an action which was taken outside the house. It does not affect the honour of the house nor the honour of the members of the house, and is more in the nature of a grievance. I regret that I see no question of privilege at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO CRASH OF T.C.A. PLANE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that the Minister of Transport has decided that a public inquiry should be held into the tragic loss of the aircraft at Ste. Therese, Quebec, on November 29, 1963, and that I have ascertained that Associate Chief Justice Challies of the superior court of Montreal is willing to undertake this inquiry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is the imention of the government to withdraw from participation in the international control commission in South Viet Nam? I ask this question in view of various news reports in the press and on the radio this morning.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM
subsubtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA FROM CONTROL COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not the intention of Canada to withdraw from the international control commissions in Viet Nam, in Cambodia or in Laos but, as I stated a number of weeks ago in the external affairs committee, we have noted the criticisms made of particular commissions, not of Canada's participation but of the commissions themselves. I stated then, and I repeat now, that Canada is not anxious to cling to this particular assignment. We have indicated to a number of countries that perhaps they would like to participate if this were acceptable to the 14 powers. It is not our intention to withdraw, but it is also not our intention to stay on against the wishes of those countries concerned.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM
subsubtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA FROM CONTROL COMMISSION

subsubtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA FROM CONTROL COMMISSION
speechtext: The decision as to which countries should compose the commission is of course a matter to be decided by the Geneva accord powers. The view of the government is that Japan, a great Asian nation, should play an increasing role in the affairs of Asia. While we understand the reluctance of that country to participate in certain situations we hope, nevertheless, that an opportunity may be afforded to Japan to play an increasing part not only in the affairs in the area which immediately surrounds her but in Asia as a whole.

subtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM
subsubtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF CANADA FROM CONTROL COMMISSION

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, this question really is comprised of two parts. In respect of the first part, I think all hon. members will be aware that annually a review of the employment statistics in each of the n.e.s. areas is carried out. I am sorry that at this late date, when the government has been in office for as long as it has, the present administration has as yet given no indication that it is prepared to move fairly quickly toward a basic rewriting or amendment of the Immigration Act.
It is not my intention today to reiterate in great detail the inequities and difficulties which have arisen as a result of the Immigration Act as it stands and, more important, as a result of the regulations made under its provisions. However, members of the committee will, I am sure, recall that this matter has been discussed on a number of occasions when detailed criticisms of the act as it exists today have been made and the difficulties which arise out of this legislation have been pointed out.
I wish to summarize some of these difficulties in order that the minister may be reminded once again of the reasons we believe a complete revision needs to be undertaken. For example, it seems to us that the regulations should be amended immediately to remove a continuing discrimination in respect to sponsored immigrants by granting applicants the right to know the reasons for exclusion, as well as a proper hearing and right of appeal when they are excluded. At the present time an administrative device is used to exclude people arbitrarily. They are refused visas. Reasons for refusal are denied the applicant, and the only appeal which is
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration open to him is heard by an administrative board composed of former administration officials who, in turn, do not give reasons for their decisions.
Some of these matters were discussed in great detail when this house considered the situation of people who had entered Canada illegally and who were detained for long periods in Toronto and Montreal. Partly as a result of discussions in this house and as a result also of publicity and condemnation in the press, the government appointed Mr. Joseph Sedgwick to conduct an inquiry. I do not wish to interfere in any way with that inquiry. I do not wish to suggest to the government that they anticipate Mr. Sedgwick's recommendations, but I do believe the difficulties we have experienced indicate clearly that it is time for a basic revision of the Immigration Act.
It is widely felt that the act and its provisions are being used to discriminate against prospective immigrants to Canada on the basis of race, religion and colour. I know-and the minister, I am sure, would remind the house if I did not say so-that the situation is much better than it was. At the same time, Mr. Chairman, I can tell the minister that very important groups of people and very important countries are still extremely dissatisfied with our attitude in regard to this question.
I have in front of me a speech made by the premier of Barbados, Hon. Errol Barrow, to the Canadian institute of international affairs at the University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, on October 25, 1963. I want to read just a couple of paragraphs of this speech into the record, because I believe it is important to the house, to the minister and to the people of Canada to realize that some of our commonwealth partners have a very poor opinion of Canada's attitude toward them. It seems to me that if the commonwealth is to mean anything, if the commonwealth is to be more than just a name, surely the Canadian government, the Canadian parliament and the Canadian people ought to do everything possible to wipe out the inequities which exist. If such inequities and injustice do not exist, surely the minister and his department have a duty and a responsibility to get across to these countries what the actual situation is, so they do not think they are being discriminated against on the basis of race, colour, religion, and so on.
I wish to read just a couple of paragraphs from this speech because I think it is not only an excellent speech but it demonstrates how the peoples and the governments of the West
8438	HOUSE OF

And now I come to what is perhaps one of the more vexed problems of the relationships between your country and ours, and that is the question of immigration. The government of Canada is responsible for the policy of immigration into this country like any other government is. A government has to lead from in front; a government cannot wait to find out what the attitudes of little isolated groups of people in that community may happen to be in order to formulate its policy. And this is something on which I am very strong. Very often people in a country cannot appreciate the reasons or the motives behind the action of a government in implementing proposals or passing legislation; but a government has to be outward looking and a government has to lead from in front. And I am not satisfied that on the question of immigration the Canadian government has ever led from anywhere but far in the rear of public opinion. The truth of the matter is that the liberalization of the immigration policy around about January or February, 1962 allowed West Indian immigrants who have special skills or who have relatives in the Dominion of Canada to come into this country without any great formality. Formalities still exist, but they are not as rigorous as they were before. Despite this liberalization of the immigration policy of this country, we find that last year only 1,500 West Indians entered the Dominion of Canada out of a total migrant entry of some 75,000 or 77,000 people. We have approximately three and a half million people in the British Caribbean and in the same period 4,500 people went to the United Kingdom from Barbados alone and, subject to correction by the Jamaican high commissioner, about 12.000 Jamaicans went to the United Kingdom. Now it is much more expensive to get from the Caribbean to the United Kingdom than it is to get from the Caribbean to the Dominion of Canada. Furthermore, I think that the West Indian would much sooner endure the rigours of a Canadian winter than the vagaries of an English summer. I have never heard a West Indian working in this country complain too much about the winter, but in the middle of summer I have heard them make some very unfavourable comments about the English weather. Therefore the proposition would have to be that the West Indian would sooner come to Canada than go to the United Kingdom. Why then do we get from two territories alone something like 18,000 West Indian workers, despite the commonwealth immigrants act of 1962, going to the United Kingdom and only 1,500, including 250 domestic servants who come out under special visa arrangements, coming to the Dominion of Canada? To be brutally frank, ladies and gentlemen, there is a feeling that in the large influx of unskilled Italian and other European immigrants coming into this country, there is either tacitly or explicitly some element of discrimination against the West Indian immigrant.
Later the premier of Barbados said:
And that is why I think that a government ought to stop hiding behind such shibboleths as housing problems and problems of accommodation, problems of integration and that kind of thing, and give the lead from in front and not trail so dismally behind.

I want to emphasize again that these are not the words of an ordinary immigrant, a person who comes to Canada and does not know what is going on in Canada, who does not know what is going on in Great Britain and does not know what are the problems of the West Indies. These words come from the premier of one of the West Indian countries. I think the people of Canada and the government of Canada owe it to the people of the West Indies, if the commonwealth concept means anything, if the democratic concept of equality of all people regardless of race, religion and colour means anything, to either correct this situation which the premier of Barbados says in his speech exists, or we need to do an educational job of explaining to the people of the West Indies why this situation exists about which the premier of Barbados has spoken.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to raise one other question with regard to immigration. We have not had as large an immigration into Canada in recent years as we had in earlier years, but the nationalities that have come here have changed very markedly. The number of people who have come from Great Britain and from the northern and western parts of Europe has dropped, certainly percentagewise, very substantially; and the number of people who have come to Canada from eastern and southern Europe, from countries like Italy and Greece, has increased very substantially.
I say this, Mr. Chairman, not in any critical sense, because I think it is obvious why the people who traditionally came here from countries like Great Britain are not coming now. I have mentioned the reasons before, as have other members. Naturally when they have full employment in western Europe, while until this year at least we have had for the last ten years substantial unemployment, people are not going to come here. Naturally people from countries like Italy, Greece and Portugal, which have a much lower standard of living than Canada, are going to come here as quickly as we permit and encourage them to do so.
This is what has happened, Mr. Chairman. I not only do not disapprove of this, I welcome it, provided the department, in co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities, recognizes some of the problems which have arisen and will arise as a result of this change and takes steps to help integrate the people who have come here so they may become what
[Mr. Orlikow.l

they want to become, namely law abiding, well adjusted, well integrated citizens of Canada.
I think they have done remarkably well. One can visit the new Canadian areas of any large city in Canada, whether it be Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver, to mention just a few, and see how well these people have become integrated. One must admit and be happy at the fact that the largest percentage of them have been able to find jobs, learn to speak English and do a better job [DOT]of integrating into our society than they were able to formerly. But the fact is that for a large number of them this integration has been very difficult. In many cases it has not yet begun, and many difficulties still exist.
It seems to me that the department must have a much closer look at the kind of people who are coming here and at the problems which have arisen. I do not think the department must do this necessarily by itself, because I recognize that to a large extent these social and economic problems are the responsibility of the provinces and the cities in which these people live. But if the federal government is going to encourage people from Italy, Greece and Portugal to come here, it seems to me that it is the responsibility of the government and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to do everything possible to see that they are integrated into our way of life as quickly as possible.
To a large extent the people who have come here from countries such as Greece, Italy and Portugal are people who do not know the language, and that is understandable. They are people who have lived under governments and regimes which were not democratic. Some were fascist, some certainly autocratic; and the knowledge of these people of democratic society, how people live under our kind of government, and their knowledge of institutions like trade unions and co-operatives is, to say in the least, very limited.
There was an excellent series of articles about immigrants in Toronto which appeared in the Globe and Mail in September of this year, in the course of which some of the problems these people face were dealt with. The fact is that many of them are mercilessly exploited just because they do not know our language, our laws and our customs. The Globe and Mail listed-I am sure it was not difficult to obtain a list because any trade union organizer in any city in Canada could
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration provide one-dozens of cases where immigrants worked here, particularly those who did not understand English, for months if not years for wages which were less than the law of the province required.
It seems to me that to say that minimum wage laws are a provincial matter is just not good enough.
If we encourage people to come here, Mr. Chairman, to work in restaurants, laundries and the construction industry; and if there is evidence-and I suggest to the minister there is ample evidence-that they are being paid starvation wages and are being exploited, I submit it is the responsibility of the minister's department to work with the provincial authorities in order to make sure that the people who are encouraged by the government of Canada to come here receive the protection to which they are entitled.
A large number of people who have been brought to Canada are working as agricultural labourers. I know these labourers come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and even if they did not one could not expect the minister to deal with labour problems, which come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. But a large number of immigrants in recent years have worked as agricultural workers in rural areas, and like other agricultural workers they do not receive the protection of the minimum wage laws, the workmen's compensation acts, hospital insurance, and so on.
I do not think it is good enough for the department to say that all agricultural workers are affected by the same kind of situation, and it is a matter which has to be dealt with by the provincial ministers of labour and the other provincial departments concerned. After all, these people came here at the urging of the federal government. They came here because the federal department established means for encouraging them to come here. It seems to me we need to establish through the Department of Citizenship and Immigration agencies and offices to protect immigrants in the transitional period until they have an opportunity to learn the language, to learn the laws of Canada and what are their rights.
It has been suggested by people who have made special studies in this field that we need new agencies, either government agencies or voluntary agencies, established in areas where these immigrants live, staffed by people fluent in the language of the immigrants to act as a liaison between the immigrants and the community. They would be able to keep track of newcomers to the neighbour-
8440	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration hood and provide them with advice and assistance which they will need if they are to become useful, happy citizens in this country of ours. There are some voluntary agencies working in cities such as Toronto, but the ability of voluntary agencies to handle this kind of complex and expensive undertaking is very limited, and certainly limited by lack of finances.
As I said, if this government is going to continue to encourage people to come to Canada, particularly people who are new to our language, our customs and our way of life certainly I will support them in this program, because I think people from these countries I have mentioned as well as other countries should be encouraged to come here. But it seems to me that if the government are to continue to do this, as they have for a large number of years now, in fairness to them the department must establish a means so these people when they come here receive the assistance they require to enable them to become useful and happy citizens.

Mr. Chairman, I want to contribute very briefly to the discussion of the citizenship and immigration estimates. I wish to take part in this discussion in order to express a few personal ideas concerning the whole problem of immigration, even if those concepts may, in some cases, seem somewhat bold.
Mr. Chairman, I think that for the federal government immigration represents a moral responsibility as well as a social one. Not only with regard to Canadian citizens but to the citizens of the whole world.
Our country has immense resources but is still sparsely populated.
Indeed, there is certainly room for a very large population, and it should be recognized that the 19 million-odd people in this country are only a very small population for such a vast territory.
On this basis, it must be recognized that we have a double responsibility, that is to maintain a buoyant economy in Canada, and also to open our doors to people from overpopulated countries who are only too glad, at this time, to find some other place under the sun where life is a little easier.
But there are many problems connected with immigration, and the economic problem is not the least one, if we consider the fact that, at this time, the department of immigration is trying by various means to attract to Canada people from other countries so
[Mr. Orlikow.l

that they may work with us in the development of this country.
On the other hand, we recognize and deplore the fact that a very large proportion of our university graduates, technicians, and all those who have attended university, are crossing the border to the south, because they are attracted by better economic conditions in the United States.
We, in Canada, are trying by every means to raise the educational standards of our people. In the province of Quebec, more particularly, we see that the government is earmarking a very large part of its resources for the educational field, but, unfortunately, we find that in the end a very large proportion of our graduates cross the border and remain in the United States where they find greater advantages and greater possibilities of advancement.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Department of Citizenship and Immigration could not give special consideration to that problem because the exodus of our graduates to foreign countries constitutes an extremely serious loss for Canada which, on the other hand, is trying to attract citizens from other lands who, in most cases, do not have the technical knowhow and who are not adapted to our culture and our economic and weather conditions.
I should like to call the attention of the minister on that particular point because I feel it is most important for us to make the necessary effort to keep our citizens, our brothers and our children but especially our university graduates whom we need so much and who will remain here if we can, within our economic system, offer them the same advantages as they would get in the United States, at this time, or at least comparable advantages. In my opinion, economics are closely related to the immigration policy we must follow in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, there is a particular problem I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It may be somewhat delicate because it has to do with the previous traditional attitude of Quebec concerning immigration.
Yet, I think it is fairly easy to explain or, if you prefer, to justify the attitude French Canadians from Quebec had, in past centuries, toward the coming of immigrants.
I think we have to go back to the year 1760, when France left Canada as such and when England took over the control of the country, to understand what has been the situation of the French speaking Canadians in a Canada which was becoming an English colony.

Having decided they would remain a French entity on this North American continent, they had to settle in the back country, I might say, and stick to the land in order to survive. And during 100 years, they categorically opposed immigration because they knew that for them, immigration, in the situation then prevailing, was a threat to their very existence and meant assimilation sooner or later.
Since that time, 200 years have passed and during those 200 years, the French-Canadian group, as such, has laid strong foundations which practically ensure its survival. Indeed, I think that survival is no longer a problem.
What is a problem at this time is to maintain its percentage within Canada as a whole. I think that is where the federal government has a very serious responsibility, the responsibility to see about maintaining that percentage. That is not easy; it is even very difficult, I know, all the more so as my fellow citizens in the province of Quebec still have difficulty in understanding the problem, and especially in considering the solutions we may put forward in order to maintain that proportion of the French speaking element in Canada.
Personally, I have come to the conclusion that the people of Quebec should completely revise their philosophy concerning immigration.
Admittedly, if Quebec maintains its present position toward such immigration, we shall definitely see the percentage of French speaking Canadians diminish compared to that of English speaking Canadians.
In my opinion, the possibilities we have of maintaining that percentage are quite limited; we should therefore take full advantage of those possibilities if we really want to attain this objective.
Personally, after analysing the situation and scrutinizing the various aspects of the problem, I have come to the conclusion that the Quebec government should partake in the immigration policy of this country. Here, I would like to call the minister's attention to a positive suggestion I intend to make. The minister of education in Quebec, Hon. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, is, I believe a highly qualified and very broadminded man, and especially he is able to speak to the population of Quebec. By his initiatives, he proved that he had the ability and the qualifications.
It is very difficult to convince the people of the province of Quebec who are over 50 years of age that such a change is necessary in their attitude toward immigration; but it is not so difficult to convince the young
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration people. If we want this mentality to develop in the province of Quebec in the matter of immigration, we must work among those who, tomorrow, will become French Canada, that is to say our young people.
There should be, and I feel strongly about this, the closest relationship between the Quebec minister of education and the federal minister of immigration, so that together they may arrive at policies liable to give the results we are all hoping for, that is the maintenance of the present percentage of French speaking people in Canada.
There are very specific reasons, Mr. Chairman, for the maintenance of such a percentage. One of them arises from the present grievances on the part of this group of Canadians in Quebec against confederation and in favour of Quebec's withdrawal from confederation. That grievance, that separatism, since you want to call it that, also originates in immigration. We are afraid, because we realize the possibility of assimilation and we cannot see any solution to that threat other than the withdrawal of Quebec from confederation, so as to form a French state, independent from the rest of the country and able to control and maintain at the present percentage the French speaking people on the North American continent.
I believe that, in view of the facts, we should try to foster the coming to Quebec of immigrants with a Latin culture. I realize it is very difficult to attract to French Canada, or any other part of Canada, French people from France, and I understand this, because France is not overpopulated-it is a country that could be compared to a garden where people live in economic and climatic conditions that are practically ideal; it is very difficult to make a Frenchman leave his own country.
Therefore, if we cannot rely on French nationals to come to Canada or to Quebec to complement the natural increase in our population in order to maintain our percentage of French speaking people in Canada, we must look in another direction. I can only think of one solution, and that is Italy. Italy is overpopulated particularly in the north. It is a Latin country. We have considerable cultural affinity with the Italians. I think that we, Quebeckers, should make a superhuman effort in that direction.
I would like the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to study the situation very closely in order to see to what extent we should bring Italian citizens to Quebec at the present time, because I believe that if they
8442	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration cannot be assimilated into the Canadian context, it they cannot be assimilated into the Quebec context, the French context as such, we should be prepared to make certain concessions. In my opinion, particularly in Quebec, we should be prepared to accept a very large number of Canadians of Italian ancestry in Quebec because, although we may not speak the same language, there is nevertheless a tremendous cultural affinity between us.
If we oould attract a large number of Italian immigrants to Quebec, it would be the only really practical solution for us to offset the present trend indicating that the proportion of French speaking Canadians or those of Latin culture is decreasing in the country.
I hope that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will duly note those remarks. If he discussed this problem with the Quebec minister of education, both of them could include in the educational program of the province of Quebec, a subject dealing with immigration that would be taught in all Quebec schools.
I feel that in the Quebec educational system at present, emphasis should be laid on the need to increase Canada's population. I believe we should make it clear to our school children that the coming of immigrants to our country is not a threat to our economy, far from it.
I believe there is an urgent need to increase our population. It is a matter of prime importance at present, if we want to overcome those economic problems resulting from the fact that our territory is too large for our small population. This automatically causes serious transportation problems which affect production costs before reaching the consumers. Canada must increase its population. Since our neighbours have a population of 200 million people, as long as we compete with that country, we shall experience difficulties, being unable to establish secondary industries requiring large investments in order to achieve mass production which is only justified in itself by a large consumption.
Our immigration policy must be revised. Quebec was right to object, in the past, to the coming of immigrants into Canada. Today, however, Quebec must bow to facts and change its attitude because its very existence is threatened, since, in the first place, the percentage of its population will be reduced considerably year after year compared to the total population of the other provinces and, in the second place, its economy may fall in
(Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John).]

value proportionately to the increase of the population in the rest of the country. Quebec's economy will no doubt continue to improve, but at a slower pace than in other parts of Canada where immigrants are welcome.
I urge all my Quebec compatriots, who will perhaps hear about the speech I am making here today, to lay aside prejudices and any purely local reason they may have against the coming of immigrants into the country, and consider more objectively the problem facing us today.
Personally, I think the citizenship and immigration department should open a larger number of offices in Italy, especially in the north, where apparently there are 525 people per square mile. I do not know if my figures are correct, but I am told that Italy numbers about 250,000 new nationals every year. There is seemingly more Italians living outside Italy than in Italy itself. If that is the case, I think we should do everything we can to attract Italians to Canada, more particularly from northern Italy.
Why from northern Italy more particularly? Because living near the French border these people have more affinity with us than those living in the south. Also, because the northern part of Italy is economically and industrially more developed, it would be easier for us to find there people more qualified and able to adjust to our Canadian complex, from an economical and industrial point of view. Another reason for which I favour the coming to Canada of Italian citizens-it may not apply to everybody, but in Quebec I think that it is an important reason-is that Italy is the seat of the Catholic church and that a large majority of Italians are Catholics. For us, in the province of Quebec, this aspect is very important. Having made those remarks, I think-
Are they practising Catholics?

My hon. friend is asking me if they are practising Catholics. I would not go so far as to suggest that they practise their religion more than we do in Canada. On the other hand, I cannot insult them by pretending that they practise it less. In any case, we in Quebec have only ourselves to blame if we do not practise more.
Do you pretend that we do not practise our religion as much as they do?

Unfortunately, I do. We must strive for perfection and, as

far as I am concerned, I realize that the goal is still to be reached. I also think that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) finds himself in the same situation.
I should like to come back to the economic question, the sore spot in the objections of most people. I believe that here, in a nutshell, is Quebec's main objection: we now have 200,000 unemployed and, if we were to accept 100,000 Italians each year, would we then have 300,000 jobless people after two years and an additional 100,000 a year later?
I feel that, at this time, it is possible, through the publicity media available, to educate the population in regard to the economy, so that they may understand that the economy of a country expands with its population, and that the more the population of the country increases, the more the Canadian economy will be buoyant and prosperous.
In my opinion, the population of Quebec can understand this reality as well as that of the other provinces. All we have to do is use television, radio and newspapers to carry out an objective publicity campaign and to put forward these facts which will substantiate my statements.
Mr. Chairman, before I conclude my remarks, I must point out that we need a larger population to settle our huge territory.
We also have a responsibility to the population of the overpopulated countries, and in my opinion we must prepare ourselves to face this responsibility by offering reasonable economic conditions and by opening wider the gates of Canada to immigrants, so that we can develop our country and build here a truly Canadian industry, owned by Canadians and in a position to compete on world markets.
We must do that, while safeguarding the rights of the French Canadian minority in this country, giving it the assurance that it will survive, that it is in no danger of being assimilated and that it will always have the place to which it is entitled, from the point of view of its percentage of the total population as well as from the economic point of view.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say something about immigration from the West Indies, possibly on the same line as that taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. Immigration from the West Indies has been poor in numbers, and I suppose this is because we have imposed restrictions. I am sorry we have these restrictions, because in most cases West
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indians speak at least one of our two official languages. They have the same ethical standards as ourselves, though I am free to admit they do not always observe them any better than we do; and, of course, they are members of the commonwealth. These ought to be sufficient reasons for us to remove restrictions on West Indian immigration. Of course I must also say we need to be careful not to remove all the restrictions, because there are many people in the West Indies who could not make a living in Canada and who would not fit into our society.
In 1952 when the present Immigration Act was passed, some 710 people came to Canada from the West Indies, and until 1955 the annual rate of immigration from that area ran at around that very low figure. In 1956 one restriction was removed and immigrants were allowed to enter Canada from the West Indies provided they were designated by the West Indian government as domestic servants. When that happened some 1,058 of them came to Canada, and during the next five years immigration remained in that range.
In 1962 the government decided it would be advantageous to remove that particular regulation and put in its place a restriction -perhaps I should not use the word restriction-rather, a regulation allowing people with certain educational standards, training and skills to enter Canada from the West Indies, and in that year some 1,480 immigrants came to Canada from the West Indies. Further, the then government sent immigration teams to the West Indies, and partly as a result of their work and as a result of the new regulation, in 1963 some 2,227 people came to Canada from the West Indies, still a very small number but at least those who came were able to fit into our society.
A total of 75,000 people left the West Indies in 1962, of whom only 1,480 came to Canada, but it is obvious there are many people in the West Indies who would like to settle elsewhere. I request the minister to review this whole problem carefully and introduce liberalizing measures which would allow entry into our society of more West Indians capable of making their living in Canada.
It would be unwise to open the doors wide and let them all flood in, because they are not accustomed to our climate and I am afraid some of them could not adjust to our system of living. However, the previous Liberal minister of citizenship and immigration said his government wanted to remove any stain of racial discrimination from the Immigration

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Act. I would hope the present minister agrees with this and will review the whole problem of West Indian immigration so as to allow more of these people who would like to come to Canada to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I listened attentively to the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard). I agree with the main part of his remarks, especially when he talked about the immigration of Italians from the north. Of course I am for judicious immigration to Canada.
Since the hon. member for Lake St. John talks about immigration for the province of Quebec, I think the Quebec government should take the necessary steps to settle those immigrants there. The other provincial governments should do the same thing. Those who want to encourage strong immigration should see to it that immigrants are well settled and looked after so that they may adapt themselves to the Canadian way of life.
I wanted to stress the fact that Italians from the north would certainly be qualified to come to Canada as immigrants.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

This is the first opportunity I have had to speak while any matter of concern to the hon. minister was before the house and I wish to extend to him my best wishes in the administration of what I consider to be one of the most important departments of government in the country, particularly at this time.
Before I deal with the estimates I should like to take this opportunity to place on record my appreciation of the co-operation, the understanding and the assistance of all members of the hon. gentleman's department, from whom I have never had anything but the utmost courtesy in connection with the various incidents I have had occasion to bring to the attention of the minister.
We have heard some interesting speeches today and I think I can safely say that my views coincide with most of the views which have been expressed, because despite what has been said to the contrary it is still my


impression that the concept of immigration in this country is very much the same as it was many years ago and that it will continue to be for years to come. I took the occasion during the lunch hour to look up in the library the beautiful inscription which appears on the statue of liberty-part of a poem by Emma Lazarus which is inscribed on a tablet there. I think these are words which the minister and his officials here in Canada could well bear in mind:
Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, The wretched refuse of your teeming shore, Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed, to me: I lift my lamp beside the golden door.
There are some who say this expresses a principle which no longer holds good. I deny that most emphatically, particularly because in the world today-and I have had occasion to speak on this subject before-we see approaching at a rapid rate numerous problems which will arise in consequence of the population explosion throughout the world. The expectation that the world population will double within 25 or 35 years must give us pause. We have in this country the area, the place, the opportunities, the resources. We have also a need for the people who will be cast upon our shores by reason of this population explosion.
I know there are some who feel there should be limits drawn on grounds of colour, race and religion. But I would point out that we are now rapidly approaching an age when the dropping of a nail somewhere in the deserts of Asia will have its impact in all parts of the world, and these divisions are not as valid as they were. I had occasion just over the last week end to fly to my constituency, a vast area stretching over the northwestern third of the province of Alberta. On Saturday in a small plane I flew north to a place called Hay Lakes which is along the route of the new Great Slave lake railway. Here I saw millions of acres of arable land. I flew low over tremendous forests waiting to be exploited. The railroad goes to the Pine Point area, a mine where a town will shortly be built. I flew over small hamlets which are rapidly becoming towns in an area where as a young lawyer 30 years ago I walked and rode in pursuit of my professional duties-an area with gas and oil, all that is needed to make a wealthy country, save only people; an area which could accommodate 5 million people with no difficulty at all. It seems to me that as time passes our statesmen will find it increasingly difficult to hold up their heads in council chambers of the world

to which they will from time to time be called unless we now direct our efforts towards bringing about a complete immigration policy.
I have been looking at the statute. I may be wrong and if so the minister will correct me, but it is my impression that we still have virtually the same statute as was on the books in the revised statutes of 1927. True, there have been some changes, additions and deletions but generally speaking much of the wording remains the same. I do not place the blame for this upon the minister or upon his officials. This is something which we as a people have neglected. We have failed to turn our attention to it. In the Peace river area, and indeed in all parts of the north our requirement is for people. We wonder whether or not we are going to secure the immigrants we need to develop our country as we did in the past.
There is no doubt that in what might be called the good old days-or probably they were the bad old days-people migrated from east to west because of depressions and difficult times. There were some who were adventurous, but mainly they were people who wanted to move because they were compelled to do so to carve out for themselves a new home and a new career. This is what caused wave after wave of settlement both south of the border and north of the border between our country and the United States.
That situation no longer prevails. We have now brought into our economic system what one might call built-in shock absorbers through our social legislation, through all the various schemes that, I think wisely, we have thought fit to place upon our statute books. There will no longer be in our country any wave of migration such as I saw in my country in 1929, such as existed there in 1914, such as we saw throughout the west in the last century and was also witnessed in the United States. It seems to me that if when the first settlers came to this continent they had found unemployment insurance, old age pensions, family allowances and all those other social benefits, the west would never have been settled and the people who live on this continent would still be living in crowded misery east of the Appalachians and around the great lakes. So to settle this area in the west and north, to fill it with the population which it requires-and I think as a nation having these empty spaces we have a duty to make them available-we will have to attract and secure the entry into this country of people from outside these limits.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I am going to be very brief in my suggestions, Mr. Chairman. I suggest to the minister this will require a new concept of the problem of immigration. I wish to make this suggestion to the minister before I sit down.
I understand there is under consideration a new act. All too often some act is formulated by a minister and his advisers, and when it emerges, it emerges as partisan legislation in the sense that it is ultimately offered by the government. I suggest to the minister that he should give serious consideration, before bringing forward any legislation, to the appointment of, or to asking the house to consider the appointment of a small select committee which could operate, possibly this year but certainly next session, to deal with this whole question of immigration, our approach to it, the question of what, if any, limitations we should place on the entry into this country of other people, the relation of our immigration policy to our economic and social problems, and in particular the necessity of settling that part of the country which lies to the north.
There is just one other matter I wish to deal with very briefly before concluding. Some other speakers have mentioned this question. I was on the island of Jamaica last winter during a very brief visit to the West Indies. Jamaica is a small island of some 3,400 or 3,500 square miles, with 1,800,000 people. It has a very small area of arable land; much of it is mountainous, much of it is unfit for cultivation and, as an hon. member said earlier, it is a country which is part of the commonwealth, a country which has many of the same principles, the same outlook and the same future as we have. This is an apt illustration of the problems which we face: To what extent should we, must we, give consideration to liberalizing our immigration laws so far as people from this area are concerned? It is my submission that this is a subject matter which lends itself exceptionally well to treatment by a committee of this house, a committee of members who are in constant touch and liaison with the people of Canada and who I think would be able to come up with some recommendations and advice to the minister at some time prior to the presentation to this house of a new Immigration Act. I conclude, Mr. Chairman, by asking the minister to give very serious consideration to this suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, I have a great interest in the estimate which is now before us because, representing the constituency of Vancouver East, I have a riding in which there
844S	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration is a strong concentration of Canadians with varying ethnic backgrounds. Although the majority are what we might term British in origin, there are in Vancouver East many thousands of people whose ethnic backgrounds are Italian, Chinese, Germanic, Scandinavian and East Indian. It therefore follows, Mr. Chairman, that I receive and have to deal with a great many questions and problems with regard to the meaning and operation of the Immigration Act, our immigration policies our immigration regulations, etc.
Over the years certain factors have stood out in dealing with these questions and problems of my constituents. The first is one that was mentioned in the concluding remarks of the previous speaker, namely that a new Immigration Act is necessary. Mr. Chairman, it is now almost becoming an historic reference to make mention of a new Immigration Act. If you go back over the years you will find that every time a new minister takes over the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the first or second speech that he makes in public, nearly always to an ethnic group somewhere in Canada, is to the effect that he is going to give priority to the overhaul of the Immigration Act and immigration policies, and will introduce a new act. Over the years I do not know of one minister going into that portfolio who has not done this within a week or two. Yet we still do not have that act.
In this respect, Mr. Chairman, the new minister is no different from his predecessors. He is kind enough to send to members of parliament copies of his words of wisdom as he spreads them across Canada in his speeches to ethnic groups. I have them. He, too, gives top priority to the need or necessity for a new act. Therefore, and rightfully so, under this estimate we can ask as top priority, will the minister tell us when the years of saying that this overhaul of the act is going to have priority are going to end, and the overhauled act will be introduced into the House of Commons for the consideration of its members? That is the first point, Mr. Chairman; because I think we have all agreed over the years-all parties and all ministers -that there is this need.
The second point is something with regard to which I believe I have considerable knowledge because of the ethnic background of the constituency of Vancouver East. Speaking from memory, over the years I do not believe I have ever raised an immigration problem with the minister or his predecessors that was not because of an approach made


to me by a Chinese Canadian, an Italian Canadian or an East Indian Canadian in my constituency and dealing with the landed immigrant status of a relative. Whether it was a wife, child, brother or sister, it was a relative. Every time an application has been made on behalf of a Canadian in my constituency- and I have had many cases because I have such an ethnic stronghold, if I may put it that way, in my constituency-dealing with the landed immigrant status of a relative, be he from Indian, Pakistan, China or Italy, what has amazed me and continues to amaze me is the length of time it takes to process the application or to resolve the problem after it is brought to the attention of the department, either directly by the applicant or when the applicant comes to me as his member of parliament and I raise it for him. I could understand a matter of weeks or even three or four months would elapse, but my experience has been that month after month after month goes by, in some cases more than a year, before these matters are processed and resolved. That is not a good state of affairs. It is not good on the basis of public relations, international understanding, or for members of parliament who are trying to handle the grievances and problems in their constituencies so far as immigration matters are concerned.
If the minister were to tell this house that there is a shortage of staff at home and abroad, or a shortage of medical practitioners in Hong Kong or in our overseas offices, and were to ask this House of Commons for the required staff when he brought in his estimates, I can assure him that I would not be standing alone to back him and to see that he gets the required staff so that we can have an efficient processing of matters affecting immigration. I also think there are many problems caused by unnecessary red tape, and I sincerely hope that some examination is being made to correct the delay in processing due to unnecessary red tape.
I want to follow this up, Mr. Chairman, with another phase, one which I regret having to mention because the minister and his department must be getting a pile of files and correspondence between his department and myself concerning cases I have drawn to his and to the department's attention on behalf of my constituents. I regret having to say this, but it is my opinion that there is too much emphasis being placed in the department on trying to find some technicality, some regulation, some specific reason to turn down an application for landed immigrant status, rather than using a humanitarian

approach in order to see whether or not it is possible to meet the desire of the applicant or to meet the proposals constructively presented by members of the House of Commons on behalf of their constituents. I say this particularly with regard to applications made by Chinese which come before the department.
I fully realize all the difficulties in the past and even some of the difficulties in the present. I fully realize the problems the department has had as a result of illegal entry, lies and confusion and contradictory statements, many of which have been cleared away now as a result of the policies regarding amnesty since 1961 or, in the cases of people who entered Canada after July 1961, the sympathetic consideration shown to them. I fully realize that these contradictions have occurred and these confusions have abounded but the more I deal with the Chinese the more I understand them. It is because these people themselves are confused and even scared. The reason for these contradictions and confusions is the fear that the ultimate decision will be a negative one. I should like to give two or three examples of this, as I think it is the best way to bring home what I have in mind. I will deal only with my constituents in Vancouver East.
After months of negotiation and the interchange of correspondence-I realize the minister had to deal with both his Vancouver office and Hong Kong and correspondence went back and forth-finally yesterday I was told that in the case of one application the answer was no, it would be rejected, and the reason was there was confusion in the mind of this old man as to the date when his son was bom, etc. This applicant is an elderly Chinese Canadian for many years resident in Vancouver who operates a small business store in my constituency. His first wife was killed at the time the Japanese went into Hong Kong. Then he married again and his second wife is here. He had a child who was born in Canada and this child is at school. But he wants to bring over to Canada one son of his previous marriage. This man is old and not well. His wife is ill. She has just come out of hospital for the second time having undergone further operations, and he wants his son to take over the store and help keep his other boy at school. He made his first application 12 years ago and I am still fighting his case. But I have been informed that the answer is no because of this old man's confusion. He has been told
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that he cannot prove tnat this boy in Hong Kong is his son.
I am sorry that he cannot prove it, and frankly I do not know how he could prove it. But this is the point. If this boy is not his son, will you tell me, Mr. Chairman, why this Chinese Canadian who has operated a small grocery store for some 12 years in my constituency has been sending this man some $50 Canadian a month for his security and maintenance in Hong Kong? He has kept all the receipts, and I cannot conceive of an aged Chinese sending $50 a month to maintain someone in Hong Kong who is not his son. As I say, he made his first application 12 years ago and still wants this young man to come over. The authorities say that although perhaps there is some truth to this, otherwise he would not be doing it, the answer is still no. The authorities say that what he said 12 years ago and what he said two months ago do not jibe, so they have turned him down. It is this attitude that I cannot understand. Surely it is the milk of human kindness to consider these cases from the humanitarian point of view rather than look for technicalities; and surely the benefit of the doubt should be in favour of any applicant. That is just one example, but I want to give some others to drive my point home.
I have in my constituency another aged Chinese. How many years he has been in Canada I do not know but I do know that for 35 years he was the No. 1 boy-that is the term they use-of one of the most well known financial and industrial families in Vancouver. After 30 years as No. 1 boy he retired. He had saved his money and he bought an apartment block in Vancouver East which he is now running. He has only one child, a son born in Canada. That son has spent seven years in the R.C.A.F. and is still in the air force as a pilot. He is away from home.
His mother-in-law is in Hong Kong and she is very old and very ill. Admittedly she is old and ill. She has only one, two or three years of life left but she has been refused permission to come to Canada to see her daughter again and to die here. She can receive all the medical treatment she needs here. The man is prepared to pay her fare and to give her all the medical attention she requires. He will put up a $1,000 or $2,000 bond if the department requires it. But the answer is no.
With her is a nephew of this constituent of mine who at a very tender age was sneaked
